answers.answer: MySQL is a relational database server, separate from the application. Clients send SQL requests; MySQL reads or changes tables and returns rows or results. Related table values let joins combine rows, and foreign keys can require references to existing related rows. Multiple applications can share one server, on the same or networked computers, fitting shared structured data. Designers still choose data relationships, constraints, queries/indexes, transaction boundaries, concurrency rules and failure/recovery requirements; MySQL cannot infer business invariants. A storage engine manages table storage, retrieval and locking. Default InnoDB supplies transactions, foreign keys, crash recovery and row-level locking. Check each table's engine because other engines have different capabilities, including whether changes can roll back. Row locks coordinate finer units than whole-table locks but conflicting operations still wait or deadlock.

evidence.quote: Multiple applications can connect to the same MySQL server.
Joins combine rows from tables, commonly by matching related values.
Manages how table data is stored, retrieved, and locked.
MySQL's default engine. It supports transactions, crash recovery, foreign keys, and row-level locking.
Row-level locking coordinates finer units than locking an entire table for every write, but conflicting operations can still wait or deadlock.

answers.answer: Types constrain the kind of stored value (INT whole numbers, DECIMAL exact decimals, VARCHAR/TEXT text). A primary key identifies a row with unique, non-null column(s); UNIQUE disallows duplicate non-null keys; NOT NULL requires a value. A foreign key requires a reference to match another table's key. An enforced CHECK rejects false conditions. A required nonnegative quantity needs CHECK quantity >= 0 plus NOT NULL. A required related-row reference needs a foreign key and NOT NULL. Verify the deployed version, CHECK enforcement and SQL mode: strict mode rejects many invalid inputs, while non-strict mode may adjust values and warn, such as 'abc' becoming 0 in INT. Declarations do not coordinate an unprotected read-then-write or infer all business rules. Atomicity commits the whole transaction or rolls it back; consistency preserves declared and correctly implemented invariants; isolation governs concurrent visibility/changes using versions and locks; durability preserves commits under configured failure guarantees. Autocommit, enabled by default, commits each successful statement separately unless an explicit transaction is open. For two dependent changes, START TRANSACTION before both, COMMIT only when the group succeeds, and ROLLBACK on failure. Constraints enforce declared validity; isolation coordinates concurrent access but does not make arbitrary logic correct. Default InnoDB flushes recovery redo at commit; delayed flushing can lose recent commits, and storage loss requires another durable copy or backup. Rollback does not undo an external HTTP effect.

evidence.quote: NOT NULL requires a value. UNIQUE prevents duplicate non-null keys. An enforced CHECK rejects false conditions; combine quantity >= 0 with NOT NULL if missing quantities are invalid.
Verify the deployed version and SQL mode, including CHECK enforcement; historical versions do not all behave alike.
Preserve declared rules and correctly implemented invariants. Constraints and application logic define those rules; MySQL cannot infer them.

Automatically commits each successful statement as its own transaction when no explicit transaction is open. It is enabled by default. START TRANSACTION groups several statements until you issue COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
By default InnoDB flushes its redo log, which records changes for recovery, at commit. Delayed flushing can lose recent commits; lost storage still needs another durable copy or backup.
Rollback covers this transaction's database changes, not an external HTTP side effect.

answers.answer: MVCC retains row versions so consistent reads can use versions permitted by visibility rules while others modify rows. An isolation level sets rules for concurrent visibility and changes. Default InnoDB Repeatable Read normally establishes a transaction snapshot at its first plain SELECT, excluding FOR UPDATE/FOR SHARE; subsequent plain reads reuse it while seeing their own transaction's changes. If another transaction changes a read price from 10 to 12 and commits, a second plain read still sees 10 unless this transaction also changed that row. Locking reads and writes follow different current-data rules, so this is not a universal snapshot promise or automatic business-race prevention. For one remaining unit, start a transaction, SELECT the relevant record FOR UPDATE, check the protected current quantity, decrement only if sufficient, then commit (otherwise end without decrement). Each contender must check while holding that protection; an earlier unprotected check reserves nothing. Conflicting updates wait for the holder to finish. Deadlocks are cycles of lock waits; InnoDB normally rolls back one participant, which must retry its complete aborted transaction under a bounded policy. Keep lock-holding work short. InnoDB's clustered index holds row data, normally by primary key. Secondary indexes contain indexed columns plus primary-key values to locate the full row. A wider primary key enlarges secondary entries, so a compact stable key often saves space subject to workload needs. Choose candidate indexes for filters/order, inspect EXPLAIN's chosen plan and measure representative queries/data. Scans can be cheaper for small tables or broad queries; an available index is not guaranteed to be chosen. Indexes can lower search work and update locks, but add storage and maintenance to every write.

evidence.quote: Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) retains row versions.
Inside a transaction, the first plain SELECT, without FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE, normally establishes the snapshot. Later plain SELECTs reuse it, while still seeing that transaction's own changes.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads and locks records inside a transaction. Check and change the protected value before committing; an earlier unprotected check does not reserve it.
Locking reads and writes use different current-data rules from snapshot reads, and locks may cover index ranges.
Retry the complete aborted transaction with a bounded policy, and keep lock-holding work short.
InnoDB stores row data in this index, normally organized by the declared primary key.
Stores indexed columns plus the primary-key values used to find the complete row.
EXPLAIN shows the chosen query plan; measure representative data and requests. A scan can be cheaper for broad queries or small tables.

answers.answer: The source accepts writes and records change events in its binary log. Replicas receive these events and apply them to their own copies. Replication lag is their falling behind the source, so reads may return older data. Receiving an event is separate from applying it; only catching up in application removes that staleness. Standard asynchronous replication acknowledges without waiting for replica confirmation. If the source is permanently lost before a surviving copy obtains the write, acknowledged data can be lost. Route delay-tolerant reads to replicas; freshness-sensitive reads need an authoritative route or evidence the selected replica applied the required change. Promotion needs an eligible candidate, prevention of conflicting source authority, and updated client routing; replication alone does not guarantee lossless failover or expand source write capacity. Local crash recovery uses engine recovery information to restore local transactional consistency. Failover changes which server serves requests. Historical restoration reconstructs an earlier recoverable state. Replicas apply source changes, including accidental deletes, so current copies are not historical protection. Point-in-time recovery uses a consistent compatible backup as a base and replays continuous retained binary-log history until the desired point, such as before the destructive change. Missing/expired log history restricts recovery; logs alone lack the required base. Test restoration and application usability and measure recovery time against acceptable loss/downtime. Neither logs alone nor an untested backup establishes that the target can be met.

evidence.quote: The source accepts writes and records changes in a binary log. Replicas receive and apply those events to their own data. Receipt and application are different stages; reads can remain old until application catches up.
Standard asynchronous replication does not wait for replica confirmation before acknowledging. Losing the source permanently before another surviving copy obtains a write can lose acknowledged data.
Safe promotion requires an eligible candidate, preventing conflicting source authority and updating client routing.

Crash recovery uses engine recovery information to restore local transactional consistency after a crash. Failover changes the serving server. Historical restoration reconstructs an earlier recoverable state; these solve different problems.
Replication can propagate accidental deletes, so another current copy is not historical protection.

Point-in-time recovery starts with a compatible backup and replays continuous retained binary-log history to a chosen point, such as before a destructive change. Logs need a suitable base backup; missing or expired history limits recovery.
Test restoration and application usability, measuring recovery time. Untested files do not establish that the required recovery point is available.

answers.answer: MySQL with verified InnoDB tables is a plausible fit for shared related records, SQL lookups, enforced constraints and coordinated transactional updates. Define types/keys/relationships, verify version and SQL mode, and put related writes in explicit transactions. Protect check-and-change workflows with locking and rechecking, keep transactions short and handle deadlocks with bounded whole-transaction retries. Choose primary keys with secondary-entry size in mind and indexes for actual filters/order; use EXPLAIN and representative measurements because indexes cost storage/write maintenance and scans may win. Read replicas can support delay-tolerant read growth, but receipt does not mean application and fresh reads require suitable routing or evidence. Replicas do not increase source write capacity, and distributing writes requires additional design. Operate the service and bound connections as well as transaction length. Agree on acceptable data loss and downtime, retain compatible backups/continuous logs and test restoration/application usability. Clarify read/write traffic and main queries, stale-read tolerance, acceptable acknowledged-write loss, write latency and downtime; also establish data relationships, transaction boundaries and recovery targets. The current information supports a candidate choice, not a proven capacity or recovery guarantee; no workload quantities or agreed recovery target are supplied.

evidence.quote: Shared relational storage, SQL queries, constraints, and transactional updates with InnoDB.
A database service to operate, connections to manage, query tuning, backups, and concurrency problems such as lock waits and deadlocks.
Indexes add write work; read replicas can lag; distributing writes requires additional design.

Clarify read/write traffic, stale-read tolerance, acknowledged-write loss, write latency and downtime. Bound connection demand and transaction length, then validate recovery targets; different deployment needs may favor another database.
Define how much data loss and downtime the application can tolerate, then test whether recovery meets those limits.
